title: Understanding California's Real Estate Agency Relationship Disclosure Requirements
content_html:
If you've bought or sold a home in California, you've likely signed a form titled "Disclosure Regarding Real Estate Agency Relationship" before you ever got to a purchase agreement. Many buyers and sellers sign it quickly, assuming it's just another piece of standard paperwork. In reality, it's one of the more important documents in the transaction, because it explains exactly whose interests the real estate agent in front of you is legally obligated to represent. Understanding this form — and the law behind it — helps you know what to expect from your agent and how to ask the right questions before you sign anything else.

Why California Requires Agency Disclosure

Real estate transactions involve at least one licensed agent, and often two or more, all of whom may work for different brokerages — or, in some cases, the same one. Without a clear explanation of who represents whom, a buyer or seller could mistakenly assume that an agent is looking out for their interests when, legally, that agent's duty runs to someone else. California law addresses this by requiring licensees to disclose, in writing, the type of agency relationship they hold with each party before entering into a listing agreement or a purchase contract.[1]

The relevant statute lays out the specific disclosure form language and requires it be provided as soon as practicable, and in any event before a party signs an offer or a listing agreement.[1] The goal is simple: everyone involved should understand the agency relationship before they commit to anything, not after.

The Types of Agency Relationships in California

California law recognizes a few distinct ways an agent's duties can be structured in a residential transaction:

  • Seller's agent (listing agent): Represents the seller only. This agent owes the seller undivided loyalty and must negotiate in the seller's best interest, even though state law also requires certain baseline duties of honesty to the buyer.
  • Buyer's agent: Represents the buyer only, and owes the buyer the same kind of undivided loyalty in negotiating price and terms.
  • Dual agent: Represents both the buyer and the seller in the same transaction. This can happen when one brokerage represents both sides, or even when a single agent represents both. Dual agency requires the informed written consent of both parties, precisely because the agent cannot simultaneously advocate exclusively for either side.[2]

None of these arrangements is inherently better or worse — each simply defines a different duty structure. What matters is that you know, in writing, which one applies to your transaction before you rely on an agent's advice about price, terms, or strategy.

What the Disclosure Form Actually Covers

The statutory disclosure form is designed to be read and signed before any offer is written. It typically walks through:

  • A plain description of what a seller's agent, a buyer's agent, and a dual agent each owe to the parties involved.
  • An acknowledgment section where the buyer and seller confirm they've received and reviewed the explanation.
  • A separate section, used later in a transaction, confirming which specific agency relationship actually applies once the parties are identified (this is sometimes called the "confirmation" portion, and it's distinct from the general educational disclosure given earlier).

Because the form is largely educational in its first part and transaction-specific in its second, you may see it presented at more than one point — once early on when you start working with an agent, and again when an actual offer is being prepared, when the specific agency relationship for that transaction is confirmed in writing.

Dual Agency: What to Watch For

Dual agency draws the most questions, and for good reason — it's the one scenario where an agent legally cannot fully advocate for just one side. If your listing agent also represents the buyer making an offer on your home (or vice versa), that agent must disclose this and obtain written consent from both you and the other party before proceeding.[2] In practice, this doesn't mean the agent stops doing their job — but it does mean they can't, for example, advise the seller on how low a buyer might go, or advise the buyer on how much room a seller has to negotiate, since that information belongs to the other side. If you're uncomfortable with dual agency for any reason, you're entitled to decline consent and instead work with a different agent whose loyalty runs only to you.

What This Means for Buyers

If you're a buyer working with an agent who found you a listing that their own brokerage also represents, ask directly whether you're in a dual agency situation and what that means for the advice you're receiving. A buyer's agent who represents only you is free to give you unfiltered advice about offer strategy, comparable sales, and negotiating room. That's a meaningfully different experience than working through a dual agent, and it's worth understanding the distinction before you write an offer. For a broader look at how offers come together once agency is settled, see our guide to making a competitive offer in Temecula Valley.

What This Means for Sellers

Sellers should pay close attention to whether their listing agent is bringing in outside buyers represented by other agents (the more common arrangement) or whether the same brokerage — sometimes the same agent — ends up representing a buyer too. Either way, the disclosure form should make the relationship clear before any offer is accepted. If you're preparing to list, it's worth reviewing this alongside the other paperwork you'll encounter, including the disclosures required about the property itself — our article on seller disclosure requirements in California covers that separate set of obligations in more detail.

Agency Disclosure Is Separate From Property Disclosures

It's easy to conflate agency disclosure with the many other disclosures involved in a California real estate transaction, but they serve different purposes. Agency disclosure is about who the agent represents. Property condition disclosures — such as the seller's written statement about the physical condition of the home, or the state-mandated natural hazard disclosure — are about the home itself. Both matter, but they answer different questions. If you want more detail on the hazard-specific piece, see our explanation of California's Natural Hazard Disclosure Statement.

Questions to Ask Before You Sign

Before signing an agency disclosure form, it's reasonable to ask your agent:

  • Who exactly do you represent in this transaction — me, the other party, or both?
  • If you or your brokerage end up representing both sides, will I be asked to consent, and what changes about the advice you can give me?
  • Is there anything about this specific transaction that makes dual agency more or less likely?

An agent should be able to answer these clearly and without hesitation. If something about the answer feels vague, that's worth slowing down for.

The Bottom Line

California's agency disclosure requirements exist to make sure buyers and sellers aren't left guessing about whose interests an agent is bound to protect. The form itself is short, but the concept behind it — undivided loyalty versus shared or dual representation — has real consequences for the advice and negotiating posture you can expect. Reading it carefully, and asking questions when something is unclear, is a small step that can prevent a lot of confusion later in the transaction.
